title: Decentralised Brands
lines: Decentralised Brands asks how autonomous organizations could share a promise without surrendering their future.
Here a brand is an institution of rules, trust, reputation, and coordinated action.
The book distinguishes genuine limits on central power from participation that leaves ownership untouched.
It develops cooperation through explicit responsibilities, selective interoperability, and meaningful possibilities for exit.
Readers gain tests for examining a proposed institution, rather than assuming decentralization guarantees democracy.

title: Participation is not authority
lines: A community can contribute and vote while one owner retains every consequential power.
The book asks who controls the name, rules, infrastructure, and accumulated reputation.
Its proposed decentralised brand preserves a shared identity while limiting any custodian's mandate.
Autonomous participants still need standards and accountable decisions.
The distinction is between useful coordination and an unlimited right to control the common future.

title: Cooperation needs selective boundaries
lines: Connection can spread both value and the failure of a shared dependency.
The book uses membranes to describe selective technical, legal, and social exchange.
A community should cooperate without automatically importing every judgment made elsewhere.
Its archipelago image preserves differences so that a local error need not govern the whole network.
Exit, succession, and resistance to capture therefore matter alongside interoperability.

title: Read the distribution of power
lines: Start with the precise definition before deciding whether a distributed network meets it.
Follow authority, contribution, infrastructure, and exit through the organizational proposals.
Neither blockchain nor voting alone establishes the institutional properties the book requires.
Decentralised Brands offers a hypothesis about resilient cooperation that must be tested in practice.
Read it to examine whether a shared promise can outlive the private power of its custodian.
